extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, patent practitioners, and academics working on Korean patent litigation and administrative review
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive guidance and procedural standards for patent administrative trials, revocation suits, civil and criminal patent litigation, and the organization and practice of the Patent Court and IPTAB in the Republic of Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the Patent Act (Article 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act's purpose is “to promote technical development by protecting and encouraging inventions and promoting their use in order to contribute to industrial growth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act aims to balance public and private interests: protect inventors while leaving inventions lacking inventive step or other patentability criteria in the public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of IPTAB proceedings (ex parte and inter partes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of IPTAB proceedings exist: ex parte (appeal against examiner decisions, patent opposition heard ex parte from March 2017) and inter partes (disputes between parties over granted rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of ex parte: appeal against rejection, trial for correction, patent opposition. Examples of inter partes: trial for invalidation, trial to confirm scope of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of IPTAB trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Main trial categories include: appeal against decision to reject an application; trial for correction (narrowing claims, clerical error correction, clarifying ambiguous description); trial for invalidation; trial to confirm the scope of rights; and patent opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category has its own statutory basis (e.g., Article 132-17 for appeal vs rejection; Article 136 for correction; Article 133 for invalidation; Article 135 for scope confirmation; Article 132-2 for opposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit to appeal examiner rejection to IPTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant receives an examiner's rejection, they may pursue an appeal within 30 days of receipt of the certified copy of the decision (Article 132-17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory 30-day deadline is strict; follow service date carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent opposition deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may request a patent opposition within six months of the publication of the grant of the patent (Article 132-2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions are a time-limited route to challenge a newly granted patent on prior art grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of hearings before IPTAB (written generally; oral on request)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings may be held orally or in writing; unless requested otherwise, hearings are generally conducted in writing. An oral hearing is held upon request from the parties or if the presiding administrative judge finds it necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should expressly request oral hearings if desired and be prepared for written-first proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and decision rule in IPTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: A panel of three or five administrative judges hears a case and participates in deliberations to reach a conclusion by a majority vote before rendering the final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect majority decision-making; strategic considerations may differ with panel size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of final IPTAB decision: non bis in idem
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IPTAB decision becomes final and conclusive, no person may demand a retrial based on the same facts or evidence; exception: this requirement does not apply where the final and conclusive ruling is a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Same facts’ = facts stemming from the same cause regarding the same right; ‘same evidence’ includes evidence submitted previously and supplementary evidence unless the new evidence is compelling enough to overturn the confirmed decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental difference between revocation suits and administrative trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Revocation suits (judicial) are adversarial and prioritize the parties' pleadings; administrative patent trials (IPTAB) are inquisitorial and handled by the executive branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials/arguments presented before IPTAB are not automatically treated as having been presented in court; parties must present arguments and evidence anew in revocation suits unless otherwise admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of examination in revocation suits (nonlimitation theory for inter partes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inter partes revocation suits, the Supreme Court upholds the nonlimitation theory: the court may examine substantive or procedural unlawfulness present at the time of disposition and may consider reasons not ruled on by the IPTAB unless special circumstances advise otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can raise and prove new grounds in inter partes revocation suits; prepare to litigate broader issues than were necessarily decided at IPTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on new grounds in ex parte revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: In ex parte revocation suits (e.g., against an examiner’s rejection), the Commissioner of the KIPO may not raise a new ground of rejection that was not raised before the examiner or the IPTAB because the applicant was not given an opportunity to submit opinion disputing the new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection is aimed at procedural fairness for applicants; the limitation applies to the defendant (Commissioner) but not to the plaintiff (applicant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to institute a revocation suit
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit may only be instituted by a party to the IPTAB trial, an intervenor in the IPTAB trial, or a person who sought to intervene in the IPTAB trial but was denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General third-party standing rules do not apply; ensure IPTAB participation or intervene before IPTAB if judicial review is anticipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for filing a revocation suit
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit must be filed within 30 days from the date when a certified copy of the relevant IPTAB decision or ruling was served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 30-day period is mandatory, cannot be extended or shortened by the court. The IPTAB presiding judge may, ex officio, grant an additional period for persons in remote areas; in practice, foreigners overseas may be granted 20–30 extra days. If the presiding judge grants an additional period after lapse of the initial 30 days, the suit will still be dismissed for lapse of the initial period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter limitation of revocation suits (original dispositions principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit can only be filed against the original disposition (principle of original dispositions), except where the adjudication itself is legally flawed (principle of exceptional adjudication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft complaints to challenge the IPTAB’s original disposition; avoid recasting complaints to seek outcomes not permitted by this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is named as defendant in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: In ex parte revocation suits (rejection cases), the Commissioner of the KIPO is named as the defendant; in inter partes revocation suits (invalidation or scope confirmation), the petitioners or respondents in the IPTAB proceeding are the defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify your adversary correctly depending on the IPTAB posture to avoid procedural defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content of a complaint in a revocation suit
rubrics_metrics.description: The complaint must detail: procedural background of the IPTAB trial; a summary of the administrative decision (parties' arguments and IPTAB’s ruling); parts admitted and not admitted among the grounds for the decision; all arguments for revoking the decision; notice of related cases; and the plaintiff’s plan regarding litigation proceedings and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach necessary evidentiary documents and administrative records (power of attorney, corporate register or certificate of corporate nationality if foreign, certificate of service of the administrative decision). See type-specific lists for additional attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-specific attachments for revocation complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Required attachments vary by case type: for revocation on rejection—IPTAB decision, patent application, examiner’s preliminary rejection, amendment, opinion, final rejection; for revocation on invalidation—IPTAB decision, original register, publication of registration, evidence relating to prior art; for scope of rights—IPTAB decision, original register, publication, explanatory documents, drawings of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully compile and append the prescribed documents to avoid dismissal or evidentiary objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of lodging a revocation suit on IPTAB decision finality
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a revocation suit is lodged, the IPTAB decision subject to revocation is prevented from being treated as final and conclusive. The Patent Court requires that the purpose of the revocation suit or appeal be notified to the President of the IPTAB without delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification safeguards interplay between judicial and administrative processes; ensure timely notice to IPTAB President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content and deadline for defendant's answer
rubrics_metrics.description: No later than three weeks from service of the plaintiff’s complaint or brief containing the specific cause of action, the defendant must submit an answer including: an answer to the plaintiff's demand; parts admitted and not admitted; detailed rebuttal; other arguments necessary to maintain the decision; notice of related cases; acceptance/denial of plaintiff's evidentiary documents; and the defendant’s plan for litigation and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing or inadequate answers can forfeit defenses or weaken procedural positions; comply with the three-week deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory hearing agenda items
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparatory hearings (often by conference call) commonly address: trial dates and number of trials; deadlines for arguments and evidence (including expert affidavits); whether to request time-consuming evidentiary methods (verification, appraisal, expert witness); designation of a technical advisor; whether to hold a technical explanatory session; whether to hold claim construction hearing first; coordination with pending correction petitions; parallel hearings with related cases; and confirmation/summary of disputed issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preparatory hearings to fix procedural timelines and narrow issues; be prepared with proposed schedules and evidentiary plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal technical explanatory session
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the hearing date, the court holds an internal technical explanatory session (usually in almost all revocation suits) in which a judicial technical examiner explains the background technology and technical issues relevant to the invention and prior arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sessions are internal (no participation by parties) and aim to improve judges’ technical understanding; expect the court to supplement this with party-driven technical review during trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing conduct and time allowance in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: During hearings, examination of documentary evidence and arguments occur with identification and sharing of key issues and oral argument presentation; revocation suits, involving complex patent issues, are usually allotted significantly more time than civil suits in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for extensive preparation and longer oral submissions; allocate time for presentation of technical and legal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Court structure and special division formation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court has five general divisions (each of three judges) and may form a special division (Chief Judge + two judges) for cases that could become important precedent, are expected to significantly influence society, or lack sufficient precedents but have similar cases pending in several divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases meeting these criteria may be reallocated; counsel should highlight precedent-significance or societal impact when seeking special division assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrated jurisdiction for civil patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Jan 1, 2016, original jurisdiction of civil patent cases is limited to certain district courts (Daejeon, Busan, Daegu, Gwangju, Suwon and Seoul Central with concurrent jurisdiction), and patent appeals go to the Patent Court; this concentrates IP litigation to specialized courts/divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File civil patent cases in the designated exclusive jurisdiction courts to comply with venue rules and access specialized IP divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: International divisions and permitted foreign language rules
rubrics_metrics.description: International divisions allow parties to make oral arguments or submit documents in a permitted foreign language (currently limited to English) when a party is foreign, foreign-language evidence must be examined, or other circumstances make the case international; consent of the adverse party is required and the court may refuse if significant delay expected. Decisions are rendered in Korean; parties may receive translations and notices of appeal may be filed in the permitted foreign language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply in writing before first trial date; expect interpretation on trial date and an official Korean decision as the basis for appeal periods; translations provided after service of authentic copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and appointment of patent judges
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no express statutory requirements to qualify as a judge in specialized patent courts/divisions, but the Patent Court seeks judges with science/engineering/IP majors, prior exclusive IP handling, or experienced attorneys/patent attorneys; terms of service in Patent Court tend to be longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization is achieved through selection and retention practices rather than rigid qualification rules; expect greater technical expertise among Patent Court judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and origin of judicial technical examiners and researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial technical examiners (dispatched from KIPO) and judicial technical researchers (court-hired) provide technical support for adjudication, focusing on issues in cases assigned to them by technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They assist judicial panels with technology background and explanatory sessions; their roles differ mainly in appointment source though their functions overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of patent lawsuits (civil/administrative/criminal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent lawsuits are classified as civil (merits and preliminary injunction cases, infringement, employee inventions, royalties, etc.), administrative (revocation of IPTAB decisions and related administrative litigation), and criminal (acts punishable under Chapter XII of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different procedural rules and courts apply depending on classification; be sure to identify proper action type and applicable remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable laws and procedures for revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Revocation suits are administrative litigation governed primarily by the Patent Act; where not provided, the Administrative Litigation Act applies mutatis mutandis, and the Civil Procedure Act applies mutatis mutandis to matters not specified in the Administrative Litigation Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation and evidence collection procedures of civil suits generally apply; counsel should be fluent in interplay of these statutes when litigating revocation suits.
